claim: When a jailbreak attack succeeds against a safety-aligned LLM, the model's safety-relevant internal representations are not eliminated — they are bypassed. The attack selectively suppresses a small subset of attention heads, and suppressing that subset is by itself enough to turn a refusal into a compliance, while other heads go on representing the harmful content even as the attack succeeds. Because those representations persist, they can be read out directly as a harmful-input detector, with no additional training, at a quality competitive with dedicated safety models.
experiments_evaluated: To address subclaim "What happens to a safety-aligned LLM’s safety-relevant internal representations when a jailbreak attack succeeds?" and the paired subclaims about elimination vs bypass, run a representational comparison study on an open safety-aligned model such as Llama-2-Chat using harmful prompts from AdvBench and JailbreakBench under two conditions: (1) the harmful prompt alone, which usually yields refusal, and (2) the same harmful intent embedded in successful jailbreak prompts drawn from JailbreakBench or generated by GCG. Use deterministic decoding, validate attack success with a human-calibrated judge, and record layer/head activations during the prompt and first response tokens. First identify a "safety representation" using only the refusal condition, for example by finding directions, heads, or sparse feature groups that reliably separate harmful from harmless prompts while controlling for topic and length using harmless Alpaca prompts plus matched benign paraphrases. Then test whether those same representations remain linearly decodable in successful jailbreak runs, and whether their geometry is preserved via CKA / cosine similarity / probe transfer from refusal to jailbreak conditions. A key control is to compare against random subspaces and against non-adversarial harmful prompts that already fail or comply. If harmfulness remains decodable at similar levels during successful jailbreaks, that supports bypass rather than elimination; if decodability collapses specifically in successful jailbreaks, that supports elimination or severe rewriting of safety representations. If only some layers lose signal while others preserve it, the claim may need refinement toward partial bypass. This experiment becomes less necessary if strong prior evidence already shows stable cross-condition decoding of harmfulness at multiple layers and with multiple representational metrics.

To address subclaim "What does the jailbreak attack selectively suppress?" run a head-level causal attribution study comparing successful jailbreak prompts to matched non-jailbreak harmful prompts on the same model. Use activation/attribution patching and path patching across all attention heads to estimate each head’s contribution to refusal behavior, measuring effects on next-token refusal logits, KL divergence to the refusal run, and final ASR. Then compute differential activity and causal effect for each head between refusal and jailbreak conditions, ranking heads by both reduced activation and reduced causal contribution under jailbreak. Include controls demanded by the field: size-matched random head sets, layer-matched random head sets, and alternative circuit-discovery baselines such as simple activation magnitude ranking or sparse pruning. Also test whether the implicated heads are specific to harmfulness/refusal by evaluating the same interventions on harmless Alpaca prompts. If a small, reproducible subset of heads shows strongly reduced causal contribution specifically during successful jailbreaks, that supports selective suppression. If suppression is diffuse across many heads or equally observed for random sets, the claim of a small targeted subset is weakened. If the same heads matter broadly for helpfulness or coherence on harmless prompts, the effect may reflect generic capability disruption rather than safety-specific suppression. This experiment could be partly obviated by pre-existing robust circuit maps of refusal heads that have already been shown to drop out under jailbreak conditions across models.

To address subclaim "Is suppressing a small subset of attention heads enough to turn a refusal into compliance?" perform direct sufficiency and necessity interventions on the head subset identified in the previous experiment. On harmful prompts that normally produce refusals without jailbreaks, zero those heads or scale them down over a sweep w in {1, 0.5, 0, -0.5} during inference and measure changes in refusal logits, KL to the original refusal continuation, and ASR on AdvBench and JailbreakBench. Separately, on successful jailbreak prompts, restore the candidate heads by patching in their activations from the matched refusal run or scaling them up, then measure whether compliance reverts toward refusal. Compare against size-matched random head ablations and against ablations of top-activity but non-causal heads. Evaluate harmless Alpaca prompts to quantify collateral capability damage. If suppressing only the targeted subset reliably flips many refusals into compliance while random sets do not, that is strong evidence of sufficiency; if restoring those heads during jailbreak reverses compliance, that also supports necessity. If large collateral damage appears on harmless tasks, the result may indicate broad impairment rather than a specific refusal mechanism. If many more heads are required, or effects are weak and inconsistent, the "small subset is enough" subclaim is undermined. This experiment would be less necessary if there already exists a replicated dose-response demonstration showing both causal sufficiency and rescue via reactivation of the same head set.

To address subclaim "Do other attention heads continue representing harmful content even when the jailbreak attack succeeds?" separate recognition from refusal execution using a reply-inversion style design. Construct paired datasets from AdvBench harmful instructions, benign controls from Alpaca, and optionally paraphrased harmful prompts where the model is instructed to answer safely, refuse, role-play, or summarize the request rather than execute it. During successful jailbreaks and ordinary refusals, test each head or small head group for harmfulness readout power independent of the output action by decoding whether the underlying user intent is harmful from that component’s activations alone. Then ablate the previously identified refusal-mediating heads and re-measure whether harmfulness remains decodable from the remaining heads. Include a control that harmfulness decoding should not merely track toxic surface form by adding benign discussions of dangerous topics and policy-analysis prompts. If substantial harmfulness signal persists in many heads after the refusal-related subset is suppressed and even during successful jailbreak responses, that supports the claim that other heads continue representing harmful content. If harmfulness signal disappears broadly once jailbreak succeeds, then the bypass account is weakened and elimination or task reinterpretation becomes more plausible. If decoding is driven only by lexical toxicity controls, the result would not support a genuine safety-relevant representation claim. This experiment becomes less necessary if prior work has already cleanly dissociated harmful-intent recognition heads from refusal-execution heads with strong causal evidence.

To address subclaim "Can the persistent representations be read out directly as a harmful-input detector?" and "Does using these representations as a harmful-input detector require additional training?" build a zero-additional-training detector from internal activations of the aligned model. Operationalize "no additional training" strictly: choose either (a) an existing direction/head statistic identified from the above causal analyses without fitting new parameters on labeled harmfulness data, or (b) nearest-centroid / template matching using a tiny fixed set of hand-chosen reference prompts rather than supervised probe training. Evaluate this detector on public harmfulness datasets such as AdvBench and JailbreakBench plus safe datasets such as Alpaca, with matched benign dangerous-topic controls. Compare token-level and prompt-level aggregation rules chosen a priori, and report AUROC, AUPRC, FPR at fixed TPR, and robustness on successful jailbreak prompts specifically. Baselines should include simple lexical toxicity filters, the model’s own refusal behavior, and a lightly trained linear probe to quantify the gap introduced by the no-training constraint. If the zero-training readout achieves strong discrimination, especially on successful jailbreaks where behavior is compliant, that supports the claim that persistent internal representations can be directly read out. If performance only emerges after fitting a supervised probe, then the no-additional-training subclaim fails even if the representations exist. If the detector works only on the same prompt templates used to discover it, distribution shift concerns remain. This experiment would be less necessary if an existing frozen-feature detector with pre-registered thresholds had already been benchmarked on standard harmfulness suites and shown to generalize across jailbreak families.

To address subclaim "How does the quality of this harmful-input detector compare with dedicated safety models?" benchmark the zero-training internal detector from the prior experiment against public or API-accessible safety baselines such as OpenAI Moderation, LlamaGuard or comparable HuggingFace guard models, and the base model’s refusal behavior. Use a standardized evaluation suite combining AdvBench, JailbreakBench, and harmless Alpaca prompts, plus a held-out set of successful jailbreak prompts crafted on one source model and transferred to others. Measure AUROC, AUPRC, calibrated FPR/FNR, and detection accuracy specifically on prompts that elicited harmful compliance, because that is where the proposed detector is most valuable. Include judge calibration against a human-labeled subset so that evaluation labels are trustworthy, and report runtime/cost if relevant. Also test cross-model portability: derive the detector from one open model’s internal features and compare to dedicated external safety models on the same prompts. If the zero-training internal detector is competitive with dedicated safety models on overall discrimination and especially on successful jailbreak cases, the claim is supported. If it is clearly worse, brittle under transfer, or only competitive at unacceptable false-positive rates, the final subclaim is weakened. If dedicated safety models dominate except on a narrow slice, the appropriate conclusion may be that persistent representations exist but are not yet practically competitive. This experiment becomes less necessary if there is already a public benchmark directly comparing frozen internal readouts to state-of-the-art safety classifiers on the same datasets and operating points.
reference_experiments: Before identifying any component, test the premise that attacks bypass rather than erase safety representations. On inputs where a jailbreak succeeded, measure activation of the refusal direction across all layers and components (attention heads and MLPs) and compare against the same requests unattacked. If a successful attack flattens refusal activation everywhere, attacks do break safety representations and everything downstream is dead. The authors find mid layers still maintain substantial refusal activation under successful attack, particularly in the layers previously identified as most safety-relevant.

Construct the paired evaluation set the whole analysis depends on. Sample benign prompts from Alpaca, collect harmful behaviours from published harmful-behaviour datasets, generate attack variants with GCG, AutoDAN, many-shot jailbreaking and PAIR, and retain only pairs where the unattacked request is refused and the attacked version succeeds. Within-pair comparison is what separates the attack's effect from differences between requests. The authors obtain 378 (Llama-2-7B-Chat) and 176 (Llama-3-8B-Instruct) usable pairs from roughly 10,000 attack samples, a 2-3% yield that caps the study's statistical power.

Build and calibrate the component-scoring instrument. Extract the refusal direction by difference-in-means and select the optimal layer, project it into each attention head's output space to score that head's contribution to the refusal signal, and classify heads by distribution overlap between conditions using two-stage filtering. Then verify the classification is not an artifact of the cut point by sweeping the threshold and the KDE bandwidth. The authors use thresholds of 0.5, find stability across 0.4-0.6, and obtain 21 ACHs and 17 SAHs for Llama-3 (416 heads analysed) and 20 ACHs and 19 SAHs for Llama-2 (480 analysed), with ACHs concentrated in layers 0-3 and SAHs in layers 5-12.

Test causally whether suppressing the identified heads is sufficient to cause attack success. On harmful inputs the model normally refuses (baseline ASR about 0%), inject a negative refusal-direction feature into ACH outputs, progressively increase the number of intervened heads, and measure attack success rate — with a matched random-head intervention as control, 10 seeds and 95% confidence intervals. Without the random-head arm the effect cannot be attributed to those heads rather than to perturbing that many heads at all. The authors report ACH intervention driving ASR to 99.5% (Llama-3) and 83.7% (Llama-2), reaching 95.0% and 81.6% at just 8 heads, against 4.0% +/- 3.7 and 10.2% +/- 11.6 for random heads.

Test whether the other head type is a real source of the persistent signal. Apply the same suppression to SAHs, this time on attack inputs, and measure the change in mid-layer activation strength using mean absolute activation across mid-layer heads. The authors report Llama-2 falling from 0.222 to 0.181 (18%) and Llama-3 from 0.0062 to 0.0053 (14%), against a reference of 0.397 and 0.0086 under unattacked harmful inputs.

Discriminate the mechanistic account from the rival explanation that the two head types simply differ in sensitivity to harmful content. Using the linearity of attention, attribute each head's activation to individual input tokens, separate the contribution of the original harmful-request tokens from that of the attack-template tokens, and compare the two head types on each. The account holds only if the types are indistinguishable on the harmful request itself and separate sharply on the attack template. The authors report medians within +/-0.15 on harmful tokens, against roughly -1.5 for ACHs and +1.5 for SAHs on attack-template tokens.

Validate externally that the persistent signal generalises and is useful. Build a training-free detector that reads standardised activations at discriminative positions via top-m aggregation and thresholds the score, then evaluate Macro-F1 on ten safety-eval benchmarks across six models from three architecture families, against both the model's own refusal behaviour and trained guard models. If the readout does not transfer, the phenomenon is a property of the two models analysed. The authors report Gemma-2B improving from 0.470 to 0.853 and Qwen-7B from 0.506 to 0.860 overall, SALAD-Bench from 0.270 to 0.976, and Llama-3-8B reaching 0.888 weighted average against WildGuard 0.880 and LlamaGuard3/4 at 0.599/0.666.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A within-intent comparison of safety-relevant representations across layers and components in successful attacks versus the corresponding unattacked refusals, capable of distinguishing retention from global erasure.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 uses the same harmful intent in refusal and successful-jailbreak conditions, records layer- and head-level activations, and tests persistence through decodability and representational geometry. This would establish whether safety-relevant information survives the attack, even though it uses broader representational tests than a single refusal-direction activation measure.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A verified paired evaluation set containing the same harmful requests in a refused baseline condition and a successful attacked condition, so attack effects are not confounded with differences between requests.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed studies repeatedly specify matched harmful prompts, ordinary refusals, successful jailbreaks, and validation of attack success. Those pairs provide the within-request comparisons needed for the mechanistic and causal analyses.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible head-level procedure for localizing and classifying refusal-suppressing versus persistent-content components, with controls that make the classification robust rather than an arbitrary ranking or cutoff.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 evaluates every head using differential activity and causal contribution, with layer-matched and size-matched random controls and alternative ranking baselines. Experiments 2 and 3 then validate the candidate subset causally and examine the remaining heads, providing a functionally grounded classification rather than requiring the reference’s particular scoring statistic or threshold sweep.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A controlled causal dose-response test showing whether suppressing only the candidate small head subset converts normally refused harmful inputs into compliance, relative to matched random-head interventions.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 directly scales down or zeros the candidate heads over an intervention sweep, measures refusal and compliance outcomes, and includes size-matched random and non-causal-head controls. It therefore tests sufficiency with at least as direct a causal intervention as the reference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Evidence that heads outside the refusal-mediating subset retain harmful-content representations during successful jailbreaks, independently of whether the model ultimately refuses or complies.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 3 decodes harmful intent from individual remaining heads during successful jailbreaks and ordinary refusals, ablates the refusal-related subset, and checks whether the signal persists. Its intent-focused controls also test that the result is not merely lexical toxicity, supplying the relevant persistence evidence by a readout route rather than by the reference’s activation-strength summary.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token-level dissociation showing that the two head groups respond similarly to the original harmful request but differ specifically in their treatment of attack-template tokens, thereby ruling out simple unequal sensitivity to harmful content as the explanation.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments compare matched harmful intents, estimate head-level differential and causal effects, and control for topic, length, and superficial toxicity. However, they do not explicitly decompose each head’s activation into original harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens, so the sensitivity-based rival remains open.
reasoning_chain: The reference requires separating contributions from the original harmful request and the jailbreak template to distinguish template-specific suppression from unequal sensitivity to harmful content.
Proposed experiments 0, 1, and 3 provide matched-condition, causal, and harmful-intent analyses, but none explicitly performs that two-source token attribution for the candidate head groups.
Without that decomposition, a difference between the head groups could still arise because they respond differently to the harmful request itself.
The team would fail to learn whether selective attack-template processing, rather than simple harmful-content sensitivity, explains the head-group difference: partial.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An external validation of a genuinely training-free internal readout across varied harmfulness conditions and models, with quantitative comparison against the model’s own behavior and dedicated safety classifiers at meaningful operating points.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 4 constructs a zero-additional-training detector, tests it on harmful, safe, benign-dangerous-topic, and successful-jailbreak inputs, and reports multiple discrimination and error metrics. Proposed experiment 5 directly benchmarks that detector against dedicated safety models, includes held-out and transferred jailbreak prompts, and tests cross-model portability. The proposed breadth differs from the reference’s exact benchmark and model counts, but the claim does not bind those counts.

sufficiency_reasoning: As a whole, the proposed set would test persistence versus elimination, localize and causally suppress a small head subset, show whether other heads retain harmful-intent information, and evaluate a no-training detector against dedicated safety models. The remaining ambiguity is the mechanistic rival addressed by reference experiment 5: the proposed results would not cleanly show that the candidate head types differ specifically on attack-template tokens rather than on the harmful request itself.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Matched harmful requests with baseline refusals and successful attack counterparts, retained based on observed outcomes, enabling within-pair comparison rather than conflating attack effects with prompt differences.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 compares the harmful prompt alone with the same harmful intent embedded in successful jailbreak prompts, validates success, and includes matched benign controls. reference_coverage.adequacy: A reproducible component-level procedure that distinguishes heads whose refusal-related contribution drops under attack from heads whose safety-relevant signal remains, with controls against arbitrary component ranking or selection.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 1 evaluates every attention head using differential activity and causal attribution, with random, layer-matched, and alternative-ranking controls. Proposed experiment 3 then tests component-level harmfulness readout in the remaining heads after refusal-head ablation, jointly providing an empirically grounded distinction between suppressed and persistent head populations.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A causal, dose-dependent intervention on a small candidate head subset during normally refused harmful inputs, with matched random-head controls and behavioral measurement of conversion to compliance.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 directly zeros or scales the candidate heads over an intervention sweep, measures attack success, and compares against size-matched random and non-causal head sets. Its rescue intervention on successful jailbreaks provides additional causal validation rather than weakening the sufficiency test.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A test that isolates the non-refusal head population during successful attacks and determines whether those heads carry a measurable harmful-content representation independent of the output action.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 3 decodes harmful intent from individual heads or small head groups during successful jailbreaks and remeasures the remaining heads after the refusal-mediating subset is ablated. Its output-independent design and controls for lexical toxicity directly test persistence of harmful-content information in other heads.

reference_coverage.adequacy: Token-resolved attribution comparing the two head populations' responses to original harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens, so attack-specific suppression can be separated from a generic difference in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments compare matched harmful and jailbreak conditions, test harmfulness readout independently of behavior, and control for surface toxicity. However, they do not attribute activation to the original harmful-request tokens separately from attack-template tokens, so a generic difference in sensitivity to harmful content remains a live alternative.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment distinguishes the mechanistic account from the rival sensitivity account by decomposing each head's activation into harmful-request-token and attack-template-token contributions.

[2] Proposed experiments 0, 1, and 3 establish persistence, head-level changes, and harmfulness decoding, but none performs that token-level decomposition or compares the two head types on both token sources.
[3] Therefore a difference observed between head populations could still reflect different sensitivity to the harmful request rather than selective response to the jailbreak template.
[4] A team running the proposed set would fail to learn whether the head-type separation is attack-template-specific rather than a generic harmful-content-sensitivity difference.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An externally evaluated, no-new-training internal readout with a fixed decision procedure, multiple harmful and safe evaluation settings, transfer beyond the discovery setting, and direct comparison with dedicated safety classifiers.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 4 specifies a zero-additional-training detector, held-out successful-jailbreak evaluation, safe and harmful controls, and fixed aggregation/threshold choices. Proposed experiment 5 directly benchmarks it against dedicated safety models, includes human-label calibration and transfer to other models, and evaluates operating-point quality rather than only raw accuracy.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set would directly test persistence versus elimination, identify and causally manipulate a small head subset, show whether other heads retain harmfulness information, and evaluate a no-training detector against dedicated safety systems. The remaining material gap is mechanistic: without separating original harmful-request tokens from attack-template tokens, the results would not fully rule out the rival explanation that the implicated head groups merely differ in generic harmful-content sensitivity.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A within-request comparison of the safety/refusal signal across layers and component types that can distinguish global erasure from persistence and localize any residual signal.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 0 compares refused and successful-jailbreak versions of the same harmful intent, records activations across layers and heads, and tests whether refusal-related representations remain decodable and geometrically preserved. That is an alternative but directly discriminating test of persistence versus elimination, with random-subspace and non-adversarial controls.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A validated paired evaluation set containing harmful requests that are refused without an attack and successful jailbreak variants of the same intent, enabling within-pair attribution of changes to the attack rather than to request content.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiments 0-3 explicitly use matched harmful/refused and successful-jailbreak conditions, while experiments 4-5 evaluate the detector on harmful, benign, and successful-jailbreak inputs, including held-out transferred attacks. The proposed set therefore supplies the paired conditions and attack-success validation needed for the analyses.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A reliable component-level procedure for identifying refusal-suppressing and safety-preserving head groups, with quantitative scoring, comparison controls, and stability against reasonable analysis choices.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 1 estimates both differential activity and causal contribution for every attention head, uses matched random and layer-matched controls, and compares alternative discovery methods. Experiment 2 tests the resulting candidate subset causally against random and non-causal heads, and experiment 3 assesses the complementary heads' harmfulness readout. These provide a causal and functional route to the same head-level specialization judgment rather than relying on the reference scoring statistic.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A dose-dependent causal intervention on the candidate head subset, compared with size-matched random interventions, that establishes whether perturbing that subset alone converts baseline refusal into compliance.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 2 directly zeros or scales the candidate heads over an intervention sweep on normally refused harmful prompts, measures refusal and attack-success outcomes, and includes size-matched random and non-causal-head controls. Its rescue arm supplies additional causal evidence, so it can establish sufficiency without using the reference intervention implementation.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A test that isolates the complementary head population during successful attacks and determines whether it carries measurable harmful-content information that remains after the refusal-mediating subset is removed.
reference_coverage.rationale: Proposed experiment 3 decodes harmful intent from individual heads or small groups independently of the output action during successful jailbreaks, then removes the previously identified refusal-related heads and repeats the readout. Persistence of harmfulness information in the remaining heads directly answers whether other heads still represent the harmful content.

reference_coverage.adequacy: A token-resolved decomposition of head signals that separately compares contributions from the original harmful request and from the jailbreak template, allowing specialization to the attack template to be distinguished from mere differences in harmful-content sensitivity.
reference_coverage.rationale: The proposed experiments compare heads and conditions at the head or prompt level, and experiment 3 controls some lexical and topical confounds, but none attributes each head's activation separately to harmful-request tokens versus attack-template tokens. A team running the set would not learn whether the apparent two-head-type distinction reflects attack-template specialization rather than different sensitivity to the harmful request itself.
reasoning_chain: [1] The reference experiment separates each head's contribution from the original harmful-request tokens and from the attack-template tokens.
[2] That separation is what distinguishes the selective-specialization account from the rival explanation that the head types merely differ in sensitivity to harmful content.
[3] Proposed experiments 1 and 3 provide head-level causal/readout and lexical controls, but do not perform this token-source decomposition or an equivalent comparison on the two token classes.
[4] Therefore the proposed set leaves the mechanistic rival explanation unresolved.
[5] The team would fail to learn whether the observed head differences are specifically attack-template specialization rather than ordinary harmful-content sensitivity: missing.

reference_coverage.adequacy: An explicitly training-free internal readout evaluated on varied harmful, benign, and successful-jailbreak inputs across task or model shifts, with quantitative comparison against dedicated safety detectors so transfer and practical competitiveness can be judged.
reference_coverage.rationale: Experiment 4 constructs a detector without fitting new supervised parameters, tests it on harmful and safe data with benign dangerous-topic controls and successful jailbreaks, and reports discrimination metrics. Experiment 5 compares that detector with multiple dedicated safety-model baselines, uses held-out transferred attacks and human-label calibration, and tests cross-model portability. The particular number of benchmarks and models in the reference is not binding to the claim.

runs.sufficiency_reasoning: The proposed set directly tests persistence versus elimination, identifies and causally intervenes on a small head subset, tests residual harmfulness information in other heads, and evaluates a no-additional-training detector against dedicated safety baselines. Thus it could resolve the main claim by multiple routes. It remains qualified because it omits the token-resolved harmful-request-versus-attack-template analysis needed to rule out the specific sensitivity-based rival explanation, so the strongest mechanistic interpretation of selective suppression would remain less secure.
